content.title: About
content.content: Kumquat is a small oval citrus fruit native to China. It is eaten whole, together with its thin sweet skin, which contrasts with the tart flesh. The flavor is sweet-tart, with a bright citrus aroma. Kumquats are eaten fresh and added to salads, sauces, jams, candied fruit, and drinks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kumquats are eaten whole, with the skin.
The name comes from a Cantonese phrase that can be translated as golden orange.
In China and Vietnam, fruiting kumquat trees decorate homes at the New Year as a symbol of luck and prosperity.
Kumquats grow on small trees and are well suited to growing in pots.

items.title: Contain vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: The edible skin provides more fiber than the flesh of other citrus fruits.

items.title: Contain essential oils
items.content: The oils in the peel give it its aroma.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Fresh kumquats are low in calories.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Kumquats are acidic and may cause heartburn or irritate tooth enamel.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Citrus fruits can cause allergic reactions.

items.title: Peel and treatment
items.content: Because the peel is eaten, the fruit should be washed thoroughly, and where possible choose fruit grown without pesticides.

items.title: Sugar in candied fruit
items.content: Kumquat jams and candied fruit contain a lot of added sugar.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wash kumquats thoroughly and eat them whole, removing the seeds if they bother you. To soften the tartness, roll the fruit in your hands and press it lightly. Slice them into salads, make sauces, jams, and candied fruit, and add them to drinks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store kumquats at room temperature for a few days or in the refrigerator for two to three weeks. Do not keep them in tightly closed bags, as mold develops. Discard fruit with mold.
